ai-apps.name: AI apps / monetization
ai-apps.what: Software that turns model capability into recurring revenue — the demand signal at the top of the stack.
ai-apps.whyMoney: Sits closest to end-user willingness to pay. Converts model capability into subscription or usage fees, capturing margin without owning compute. Network effects and workflow lock-in can sustain pricing power once a product is embedded in enterprise or consumer workflows.
ai-apps.whyFail: Thin moat if the underlying model is commoditized or replicated by a competitor with cheaper API access. Hyperscalers can bundle equivalent features. Customer acquisition costs may outpace lifetime value if churn is high and switching costs are low.
ai-apps.bottleneck: Demonstrated, repeatable ROI for paying customers. Enterprises require measurable productivity or cost savings before expanding seats; without proof, sales cycles stall and net revenue retention deteriorates.
ai-apps.metrics:
Net revenue retention rate
Gross margin on software revenue
Annual recurring revenue growth rate
Customer acquisition cost vs. lifetime value ratio
Free-to-paid conversion rate
ai-apps.redFlags:
Gross margins compressing toward infrastructure-like levels
Revenue concentrated in a single model provider's API
High churn masked by new logo growth
Hyperscaler launches a native competing feature
Licensing terms from model providers tighten or reprice

model-labs.name: Model labs / AI platforms
model-labs.what: Frontier model developers and AI platforms — the buyers driving compute demand (most are private: OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI).
model-labs.whyMoney: Frontier model capability commands premium API pricing and platform fees. First-mover scale advantages in training data, RLHF pipelines, and researcher talent create temporary scarcity rents. Platforms that host third-party models also earn a toll on every inference call.
model-labs.whyFail: Compute costs are largely variable and scale with usage, compressing margins. Open-weight models can erode API pricing floors. Most leading labs are private, limiting public-market access. Regulatory intervention on safety or data use could constrain operations.
model-labs.bottleneck: Access to sufficient high-quality training data and frontier compute at acceptable cost. Diminishing returns on scale-up, or a capability plateau, would undermine the investment thesis that more compute equals better monetizable models.
model-labs.metrics:
API revenue and growth rate
Cost per token (training and inference)
Model benchmark rankings relative to peers
Developer ecosystem size (active API keys, third-party integrations)
Compute spend as a share of revenue
model-labs.redFlags:
Sustained inability to convert research capability into revenue
Open-weight model matches proprietary performance at near-zero marginal cost
Key researcher attrition to competitors
Regulatory action restricting training data or deployment
Compute costs rising faster than API pricing power

hyperscalers.name: Hyperscalers / cloud capex
hyperscalers.what: Cloud platforms financing the buildout on balance sheet and renting it back as capacity.
hyperscalers.whyMoney: Own the customer relationship, billing infrastructure, and data gravity. Rent GPU capacity, storage, and networking at a markup over their own capex cost. Long-term enterprise contracts provide revenue visibility. AI workloads carry higher average selling prices than general compute.
hyperscalers.whyFail: Massive upfront capex creates fixed-cost leverage that punishes utilization shortfalls. If AI workload growth slows or customers repatriate workloads on-premises, returns on invested capital deteriorate. Antitrust scrutiny on bundling practices is a structural risk.
hyperscalers.bottleneck: Power and physical data-center space. Permitting timelines, grid interconnection queues, and cooling constraints limit how quickly new capacity can be brought online regardless of capital availability.
hyperscalers.metrics:
Cloud segment revenue growth and operating margin
Capex as a percentage of revenue
Data-center power capacity under contract (MW)
AI-specific revenue or workload disclosures
Return on invested capital trend
hyperscalers.redFlags:
Capex growth persistently outpacing revenue growth
Utilization rates declining on new GPU capacity
Power procurement delays slipping announced timelines
Enterprise customers publicly shifting to on-premises AI
Regulatory forced unbundling of cloud and AI services

neoclouds.name: Neoclouds / AI cloud capacity
neoclouds.what: Pure-play GPU clouds renting accelerated capacity — high growth, heavily debt- and lease-financed.
neoclouds.whyMoney: Offer GPU capacity without hyperscaler minimums or lock-in, attracting startups and model labs. Spot and reserved pricing on scarce accelerators can command significant premiums during supply-constrained periods. Specialization in AI workloads reduces operational overhead per GPU.
neoclouds.whyFail: Business model depends on sustained GPU scarcity. Heavy reliance on debt and lease financing means rising interest rates or covenant breaches can impair operations quickly. Hyperscalers can undercut on price when their own utilization softens.
neoclouds.bottleneck: Access to allocations of leading-edge accelerators from chip vendors. Without priority supply relationships, neoclouds cannot grow capacity or refresh hardware competitively.
neoclouds.metrics:
GPU utilization rate
Revenue per GPU per day
Debt-to-equity or lease-liability-to-asset ratio
Customer concentration (top 5 customers as share of revenue)
Contract backlog duration
neoclouds.redFlags:
Utilization falling below levels needed to service debt
Customer concentration in one or two model labs
Hardware refresh cycle creating large near-term capex obligations
Hyperscaler spot pricing undercutting neocloud rates
Lease or credit facility covenant violations

gpus.name: GPUs / accelerators
gpus.what: Merchant accelerators — GPUs and AI training/inference chips sold to anyone building compute. The horsepower the whole buildout is measured in.
gpus.whyMoney: Every token trained or served runs on this silicon. Pricing power while demand outruns supply; full-stack players capture software and networking margin on top of the die.
gpus.whyFail: Merchant silicon is a target: hyperscalers design around you with ASICs, a model-efficiency breakthrough cuts compute intensity, or an overbuild leaves a glut of last-gen parts. Margins this high invite attack.
gpus.bottleneck: Leading-edge wafer + CoWoS packaging + HBM allocation. Whoever controls the software ecosystem (CUDA) controls switching costs.
gpus.metrics:
Data-center revenue YoY
Gross margin — sustained above 70%?
Supply / purchase commitments
Software + networking attach rate
Hyperscaler ASIC share shift
gpus.redFlags:
Gross-margin compression
Last-gen channel / inventory build
Hyperscaler in-house silicon ramps
Top-4 customer concentration

custom-silicon.name: Custom silicon / ASICs
custom-silicon.what: ASIC arms dealers that help hyperscalers design their own accelerators — paid on design wins, not merchant chips.
custom-silicon.whyMoney: Hyperscalers pay design fees and NRE (non-recurring engineering) charges to reduce dependence on merchant accelerators and optimize total cost of ownership. Revenue is recognized on design wins and volume ramp royalties, providing durable income streams tied to chip lifecycles.
custom-silicon.whyFail: Customer concentration is inherent — losing one hyperscaler relationship can remove a large share of revenue. Hyperscalers may build internal design teams over time, reducing outsourced design spend. Long design cycles mean revenue is lumpy and delayed.
custom-silicon.bottleneck: Specialized engineering talent in custom accelerator architecture. The pool of engineers with relevant silicon design and AI workload expertise is limited, constraining how many concurrent design programs can be staffed.
custom-silicon.metrics:
Number of active design wins
NRE and royalty revenue mix
Revenue per design program
Customer concentration ratio
Time from design win to volume production
custom-silicon.redFlags:
Hyperscaler customer announces intent to build fully internal design capability
Design win pipeline shrinking year over year
Key engineering talent departing to competitors or customers
Tape-out delays pushing revenue recognition into future periods
ASIC performance failing to meet customer TCO targets vs. merchant chips

semi-ip.name: Semiconductor IP / chiplets / NoC
semi-ip.what: Licensable IP — CPU/NPU cores, chiplet and network-on-chip interconnect — earning royalty per chip shipped.
semi-ip.whyMoney: Royalty-per-chip model means revenue scales with industry volume without proportional cost increases. Licensees bear manufacturing and design risk; IP holders collect a toll on every chip shipped. AI chip complexity increases the number of licensed IP blocks per design.
semi-ip.whyFail: Open-source IP alternatives or in-house development by large customers can erode the licensable market. A single dominant architecture standard could consolidate pricing power away from smaller IP vendors. Litigation over IP validity is a recurring structural risk.
semi-ip.bottleneck: Continued technical differentiation of licensed IP versus open alternatives. If open-source cores reach parity on performance-per-watt, the pricing premium for proprietary licenses compresses.
semi-ip.metrics:
Royalty revenue per chip shipped
New license agreements signed per period
Royalty backlog (contracted but not yet shipped)
Share of AI chip designs incorporating licensed IP
Litigation expense as a share of revenue
semi-ip.redFlags:
Major customer announces migration to open-source or internally developed IP
Royalty rates declining on contract renewals
Court ruling invalidating a core patent
Concentration of royalty revenue in a single chip program
EDA vendors bundling competing IP at no incremental cost

eda.name: EDA / chip design software
eda.what: The software chips are designed in — a duopoly that taxes every tape-out and AI-design flow.
eda.whyMoney: Chip designers cannot tape out without EDA tools; the market is a structural duopoly. Annual subscription and multi-year enterprise license agreements provide predictable recurring revenue. AI-driven design automation adds new product lines that command incremental fees.
eda.whyFail: Customer base is concentrated among a relatively small number of large chip companies. A prolonged semiconductor downturn reduces tape-out activity and delays license renewals. Open-source EDA tools, while currently limited, represent a long-run structural threat.
eda.bottleneck: Complexity of advanced-node design rules. As nodes shrink, EDA tool development costs rise, but so does customer dependency, reinforcing the duopoly. The bottleneck is sustaining R&D investment to stay ahead of design-rule complexity.
eda.metrics:
Annual recurring revenue and backlog
Renewal rate on enterprise licenses
Tape-out volume at leading-edge nodes
R&D spend as a share of revenue
AI-design-flow product revenue as a share of total
eda.redFlags:
Semiconductor industry capex cycle turning down sharply
Major customer insourcing EDA tool development
Regulatory review of duopoly pricing practices
Open-source EDA tool achieving leading-edge node certification
R&D investment falling behind design-rule complexity growth

foundries.name: Foundries
foundries.what: Leading-edge manufacturing — the physical scarcity gate for every advanced chip.
foundries.whyMoney: Physical scarcity of leading-edge manufacturing capacity creates pricing power. Long-term wafer supply agreements with take-or-pay provisions lock in revenue. Customers bear design and demand risk; foundries earn on wafer starts regardless of end-market outcome.
foundries.whyFail: Fab construction requires multi-year lead times and capital outlays measured in tens of billions. Geopolitical concentration of leading-edge capacity creates supply-chain and regulatory risk. A demand shortfall after capacity expansion destroys returns on invested capital.
foundries.bottleneck: Availability of extreme ultraviolet lithography equipment and the specialized supply chain supporting it. A single dominant equipment supplier constrains how quickly global leading-edge capacity can expand.
foundries.metrics:
Leading-edge wafer capacity utilization rate
Capex-to-revenue ratio
Wafer average selling price trend
Customer long-term agreement coverage as a share of capacity
Yield rate at leading-edge nodes
foundries.redFlags:
Utilization rates declining on newly commissioned leading-edge capacity
EUV equipment delivery delays extending beyond announced timelines
Geopolitical restrictions on equipment export or customer access
Customer design wins shifting to a competing foundry node
Government subsidy dependence masking true economic returns

packaging.name: Advanced packaging
packaging.what: Advanced packaging (CoWoS, HBM stacking) — the current binding constraint on GPU supply.
packaging.whyMoney: CoWoS and HBM stacking are physically scarce processes controlled by a handful of fabs. Customers pay steep premiums and accept long lead times because no alternative path exists to high-bandwidth compute. Scarcity converts process know-how and installed capacity into durable pricing power for whoever holds the tools and yields.
packaging.whyFail: Capacity additions are lumpy and capital-intensive; a demand air pocket leaves fabs with stranded depreciation. A single large customer defecting to an alternative substrate or in-house packaging erodes utilization fast. Yield learning curves are slow, so cost reduction lags revenue, compressing margins during ramp.
packaging.bottleneck: TSMC CoWoS interposer capacity is the binding physical constraint. Lithography tools, specialized bonding equipment, and trained process engineers cannot be replicated quickly. Even with capital committed, new capacity takes multiple years to qualify and ramp, making near-term supply inelastic.
packaging.metrics:
CoWoS wafer starts per month (industry aggregate)
HBM attach rate per AI accelerator shipped
Packaging yield rates at leading fabs
Lead times quoted to tier-1 customers
Capex committed to advanced packaging vs. prior year
packaging.redFlags:
Customer concentration above 50% of a fab's advanced packaging revenue
Emergence of a credible alternative substrate bypassing CoWoS
Sudden demand slowdown leaving capacity additions half-utilized
Geopolitical restriction on interposer materials or equipment
Yield stagnation signaling process maturity ceiling

memory.name: HBM / DRAM / NAND / storage
memory.what: HBM/DRAM/NAND — bandwidth-starved AI turns memory into the new tight oligopoly.
memory.whyMoney: AI workloads are memory-bandwidth-bound, making HBM a non-substitutable component. A tight oligopoly of DRAM producers controls supply. Inelastic demand from hyperscalers and accelerator vendors lets producers sustain elevated pricing through cycles, while NAND benefits from storage density requirements in inference infrastructure.
memory.whyFail: Memory markets are historically cyclical; coordinated overinvestment by oligopoly members has repeatedly crashed prices. HBM capacity additions, once online, can overshoot demand. A shift in model architecture reducing memory bandwidth requirements would structurally deflate the HBM premium.
memory.bottleneck: HBM stacking yield and the shared CoWoS packaging step constrain output independently of wafer starts. DRAM process node transitions require massive synchronized capex. The binding constraint shifts between fab capacity, packaging slots, and substrate supply depending on the cycle phase.
memory.metrics:
HBM GB shipped per quarter vs. prior year
HBM ASP trend relative to standard DRAM
DRAM industry capacity utilization rate
NAND bit shipment growth vs. storage demand growth
Inventory days at major producers
memory.redFlags:
Inventory build at hyperscaler customers signaling demand pull-forward
New entrant qualifying HBM-equivalent product at lower cost
Architectural shift to compute-near-memory reducing off-chip bandwidth need
Synchronized capex expansion by all three major DRAM producers simultaneously
Export controls disrupting supply chains for key producers

networking.name: Networking / Ethernet / InfiniBand
networking.what: The fabric that lashes thousands of accelerators into one machine — switches, NICs, retimers, and the Ethernet-vs-InfiniBand standards war for the AI back-end.
networking.whyMoney: Scale-up and scale-out clusters need exponentially more interconnect per GPU. Owning the switch silicon, the retimer, or the reference design earns content that grows faster than GPU units.
networking.whyFail: Standards risk (proprietary fabrics lose to open Ethernet, or the reverse), in-house switch silicon at hyperscalers, and being a single-product supplier a merchant vendor designs out.
networking.bottleneck: Bandwidth per rack and signal integrity at 224G; copper reach limits forcing optical. Design-win lock-in at the cluster-architecture level.
networking.metrics:
AI back-end port share
Content $/GPU trend
Named-hyperscaler design wins
800G to 1.6T transition timing
networking.redFlags:
Customer in-sourcing of switching
Single-customer concentration
Lumpy hyperscaler order timing

optical.name: Optical interconnect / silicon photonics
optical.what: Optical transceivers and silicon photonics — moving data between racks at the speed of light as copper runs out of reach.
optical.whyMoney: Copper reaches physical limits at high data rates over rack-scale distances. Optical transceivers and silicon photonics become mandatory, not optional, as cluster sizes grow. Suppliers capture value through component pricing, integration complexity, and the engineering cost of qualifying alternatives, creating switching costs once designed in.
optical.whyFail: Transceiver markets have historically been commoditized by Asian ODMs driving down ASPs. Silicon photonics integration is technically difficult; yield and cost targets may take longer to hit than capital cycles allow. A co-packaged optics standard shift can strand prior-generation inventory and tooling investment.
optical.bottleneck: Wafer-level integration of photonic and electronic components on a single die remains a yield and process challenge. Specialized III-V materials for lasers are sourced from a narrow supplier base. Co-packaged optics adoption requires coordinated redesign of switch ASICs, creating a chicken-and-egg qualification delay.
optical.metrics:
400G/800G transceiver ASP trend
Co-packaged optics design wins at switch ASIC vendors
Silicon photonics wafer yield at leading fabs
Data-center optical port count growth vs. copper port count
Lead times for high-speed transceiver modules
optical.redFlags:
Sustained ASP erosion driven by low-cost module entrants
Co-packaged optics standard fragmentation delaying adoption
Hyperscaler vertical integration into transceiver manufacturing
III-V laser material supply disruption
Customer inventory correction after over-ordering during a supply crunch

cxl.name: CXL / memory pooling
cxl.what: Memory pooling and disaggregation fabric — early, optionality-rich, IP-led.
cxl.whyMoney: CXL enables memory disaggregation, letting operators pool expensive DRAM across servers and reduce stranded capacity. IP licensors and early silicon vendors capture value through royalties and design-win lock-in before the market standardizes. Optionality is high because the total addressable market scales with data-center memory spend.
cxl.whyFail: CXL adoption depends on OS, hypervisor, and application stack support that matures slowly. If hyperscalers build proprietary memory fabric instead, the standard loses its anchor customers. Latency penalties versus local DRAM may be unacceptable for latency-sensitive inference, limiting use cases.
cxl.bottleneck: Software ecosystem maturity is the binding adoption constraint. Hardware interoperability across multiple vendors requires sustained consortium coordination. Without broad OS-level memory tiering support, the hardware value proposition cannot be realized by most operators.
cxl.metrics:
Number of CXL-certified devices from distinct vendors
Hyperscaler public deployment announcements referencing CXL
OS kernel releases with native CXL memory tiering support
CXL IP licensing revenue at consortium members
Latency penalty of CXL-attached memory vs. local DRAM in published benchmarks
cxl.redFlags:
Hyperscaler defection to a proprietary interconnect standard
CXL version fragmentation preventing cross-vendor interoperability
Latency benchmarks showing penalty too large for inference workloads
Low consortium membership renewal or participation rates
Silicon vendor exits from CXL product roadmaps

servers.name: Servers / racks / ODMs
servers.what: ODMs and system integrators that bolt GPUs, memory and networking into finished racks.
servers.whyMoney: ODMs and system integrators earn margin on the assembly, thermal engineering, and supply-chain orchestration required to turn discrete components into qualified, deployable racks. Hyperscaler capex flows through this layer at scale. Complexity of liquid cooling and high-density power delivery creates engineering differentiation and repeat business.
servers.whyFail: ODM margins are structurally thin and competed away as designs commoditize. Hyperscalers increasingly design their own rack specifications, reducing integrator discretion. Component shortages upstream can strand finished-goods inventory or force costly redesigns mid-cycle.
servers.bottleneck: GPU and HBM allocation from upstream suppliers is the binding constraint on server output, not assembly capacity. Thermal and power delivery engineering for high-TDP accelerators is a secondary bottleneck as rack density increases beyond conventional cooling limits.
servers.metrics:
AI server revenue as share of total server market
ODM gross margin trend over trailing four quarters
Backlog-to-revenue ratio at major ODMs
Liquid cooling attach rate on new AI rack shipments
Hyperscaler capex guidance vs. ODM order intake
servers.redFlags:
Hyperscaler vertical integration into rack manufacturing reducing ODM addressable market
GPU allocation cuts flowing through to ODM revenue shortfalls
Inventory write-downs from stranded components after demand shift
Margin compression below historical floor due to competitive bidding
Single-customer revenue concentration above 40%

dc-realestate.name: Data-center real estate / colocation
dc-realestate.what: Colocation and wholesale landlords leasing powered shells — long-dated, contracted, increasingly power-gated.
dc-realestate.whyMoney: Powered shell scarcity in key markets lets landlords charge premium rents and lock tenants into long-dated leases with contractual escalators. Power availability, not land, is the gating input, so operators with secured utility agreements hold a durable asset. Long lease durations provide predictable cash flows that support capital recycling.
dc-realestate.whyFail: Power procurement delays or utility denials can strand developed land with no revenue. Overbuilding in secondary markets compresses yields. A structural shift to edge or distributed inference could reduce hyperscaler demand for large centralized campuses. Rising construction and financing costs can erode development returns.
dc-realestate.bottleneck: Utility power interconnection queue length and transformer delivery lead times are the binding constraints on new supply. Permitting timelines in constrained markets add further delay. These factors make new powered capacity effectively inelastic over a two-to-four-year horizon.
dc-realestate.metrics:
Powered shell vacancy rate in tier-1 markets
Power purchase agreement pricing trend per MW
Utility interconnection queue backlog by region
Lease duration weighted average at signing
Development yield spread over financing cost
dc-realestate.redFlags:
Utility moratoriums on new large-load interconnections in key markets
Hyperscaler lease cancellations or right-sizing of reserved capacity
Rising construction costs compressing development yields below hurdle rates
Regulatory caps on data-center power consumption in major jurisdictions
Concentration of expiring leases in a single year creating re-leasing risk

power-gen.name: Power generation
power-gen.what: The electrons. Independent power producers, nuclear fleets and turbine OEMs supplying the gigawatts data centers now compete with the grid for.
power-gen.whyMoney: AI demand turns power from a commodity into a scarce, contracted asset. Behind-the-meter and PPA deals with hyperscalers lock in long-dated, premium-priced cash flows.
power-gen.whyFail: Interconnection queues and permitting stall delivery; rate-case and regulatory risk; a demand air-pocket if AI capex pauses re-exposes merchant capacity to low power prices.
power-gen.bottleneck: Firm 24/7 carbon-free power near fiber and water. Interconnection timelines (3-5 yrs) and turbine/transformer lead times are the real gate.
power-gen.metrics:
Contracted PPA capacity (GW) and tenor
Power-price realization
Data-center pipeline (MW)
Interconnection queue position
Leverage / cost of debt
power-gen.redFlags:
Merchant exposure if AI demand slips
Rising leverage to fund builds
Regulatory pushback on co-location

grid.name: Grid / transmission / transformers / switchgear
grid.what: Transmission, transformers and switchgear — the supply-constrained plumbing between generation and the rack.
grid.whyMoney: Transformers, switchgear, and transmission equipment are manufactured by a small number of specialized producers with multi-year order backlogs. Data-center load growth is a structural demand driver layered on top of grid modernization and electrification. Scarcity of large power transformers in particular allows producers to sustain elevated pricing and long-term contracts.
grid.whyFail: Grid equipment markets are regulated and subject to political intervention on pricing. New entrants or reshoring initiatives could add supply faster than expected. Demand could soften if AI efficiency gains reduce per-rack power draw materially, slowing utility interconnection requests.
grid.bottleneck: Large power transformer manufacturing capacity is the most acute physical bottleneck. Core steel lamination, specialized winding, and long factory cycle times mean lead times extend to multiple years. This cannot be resolved quickly even with significant capital commitment.
grid.metrics:
Large power transformer delivery lead times (months)
Switchgear order backlog at major producers
Utility capital expenditure on transmission infrastructure
Number of active data-center interconnection requests to regional grid operators
Core electrical steel production capacity utilization
grid.redFlags:
Government price controls on transformer or switchgear markets reducing producer incentive
Rapid AI efficiency improvement reducing MW-per-exaflop, softening demand
New manufacturing entrants qualifying large transformer production at scale
Geopolitical disruption to core steel or copper supply chains
Utility demand forecasting errors leading to overbuild and contract renegotiation

ups.name: UPS / backup power / batteries
ups.what: UPS, backup generation and battery systems keeping racks alive through transients and outages.
ups.whyMoney: Every powered rack requires backup power; UPS and battery systems are non-discretionary infrastructure spend. Rising rack power density increases the per-unit value of UPS equipment. Battery chemistry improvements and lithium-ion adoption in data centers expand the addressable market for suppliers with qualified products and service networks.
ups.whyFail: UPS markets are competitive with multiple established global suppliers. Battery cost deflation, if sustained, compresses system ASPs even as unit volumes grow. A shift to grid-scale storage or alternative power architectures could reduce the role of traditional UPS in future data-center designs.
ups.bottleneck: Lithium-ion battery cell supply and the availability of battery management system components constrain UPS capacity expansion. High-power-density UPS units also require specialized power electronics that share supply chains with EV and grid storage markets, creating cross-sector competition for components.
ups.metrics:
UPS system ASP trend by power rating tier
Lithium-ion battery cell cost per kWh for stationary applications
Data-center UPS market unit shipment growth year over year
Service contract attach rate and renewal rate at major suppliers
Lead times for high-density UPS modules above 500 kW
ups.redFlags:
Battery cell supply diversion to automotive sector causing UPS delivery delays
New data-center power architectures bypassing traditional UPS topology
ASP erosion from low-cost regional competitors entering tier-1 markets
Customer shift to utility-side grid storage reducing on-site UPS requirements
Component shortages in power electronics shared with EV supply chains

cooling.name: Cooling / thermal management
cooling.what: Liquid and thermal management — rising power density is making air cooling obsolete.
cooling.whyMoney: Rising rack power density makes legacy air cooling physically inadequate, forcing mandatory upgrades. Vendors of liquid cooling systems, coolant distribution units, and immersion tanks capture recurring spend as operators retrofit existing facilities and spec new builds around thermal limits rather than floor space.
cooling.whyFail: Cooling is a component cost, not a platform; hyperscalers may vertically integrate or commoditize designs. Proprietary coolant chemistries risk standardization pressure. A slowdown in GPU density scaling reduces urgency. Water-use regulations could constrain deployment in key markets.
cooling.bottleneck: Skilled installation labor and facility retrofitting pace are the binding constraints. Liquid cooling requires plumbing, leak detection, and facility modifications that cannot be parallelized easily, slowing adoption even when hardware and capital are available.
cooling.metrics:
Liquid cooling share of new data center capacity (% of MW)
Average rack power density in new builds (kW per rack)
Retrofit backlog and lead times reported by major vendors
Water usage effectiveness (WUE) trends at large operators
cooling.redFlags:
Hyperscalers publishing proprietary in-house cooling designs
Emergence of a dominant low-cost commodity standard undercutting margins
GPU power-per-chip scaling plateauing, reducing urgency
Regulatory water-use restrictions halting projects in major markets
Customer concentration risk if a few large operators dominate order books

construction.name: Construction / engineering / infra services
construction.what: EPC and infrastructure services that actually build the data centers, substations and transmission.
construction.whyMoney: Every dollar of data center, substation, and transmission investment requires engineering, procurement, and construction services. EPC firms and specialty contractors capture value through project fees, margin on materials procurement, and long-duration contracts that are difficult to displace mid-project.
construction.whyFail: EPC is a services business with thin margins and high execution risk. Labor shortages, permitting delays, and supply chain disruptions compress margins or cause contract losses. Clients may self-perform or shift to modular prefabrication, reducing scope for traditional contractors.
construction.bottleneck: Qualified electrical and civil labor, particularly high-voltage substation specialists, is the binding constraint. Permitting and grid interconnection queues add multi-year delays that no amount of capital can easily accelerate.
construction.metrics:
Data center construction starts and completions (MW per quarter)
Substation and grid interconnection queue length and wait times
Labor availability indices for electrical and civil trades
Project cost inflation relative to original contract values
construction.redFlags:
Widespread project cancellations or deferrals by major operators
Surge in contract disputes or cost-overrun disclosures
Permitting reform stalling at federal or state level
New entrants commoditizing modular prefabrication at scale
Concentration of backlog in a single geography or customer

materials.name: Raw materials / specialty chemicals
materials.what: Copper, rare earths and specialty inputs — the raw-material long tail of the buildout.
materials.whyMoney: Copper, rare earths, and specialty chemicals are consumed in fixed ratios per unit of compute infrastructure built. Suppliers with low-cost, permitted, and scalable production capture pricing power when demand growth outpaces new supply, which has long lead times due to mine development cycles.
materials.whyFail: Commodity prices are cyclical and mean-reverting. New mine supply, recycling advances, or material substitution can erode pricing power. Geopolitical concentration of supply creates both opportunity and disruption risk. Demand can fall sharply if data center buildout slows.
materials.bottleneck: Mine permitting and development timelines of five to fifteen years are the binding constraint on new primary supply. Recycling and urban mining can partially offset but cannot ramp at the speed of a demand surge.
materials.metrics:
Copper and rare earth spot prices and inventory levels
Mine development pipeline (permitted projects, years to production)
Recycling recovery rates for key materials
Import concentration ratios for critical inputs by country
materials.redFlags:
Export restrictions or tariffs imposed by major producing nations
Rapid substitution of a key material by an alternative technology
Speculative inventory buildup masking real demand weakness
Environmental litigation halting major permitted projects
Single-country supply concentration exceeding historical norms

semi-equip.name: Semiconductor equipment / test / metrology
semi-equip.what: The tools that make the chips — deposition, etch, litho, test and metrology oligopolies.
semi-equip.whyMoney: Chipmakers cannot produce advanced semiconductors without specialized deposition, etch, lithography, and metrology tools. The equipment market is highly concentrated, creating oligopoly pricing power. Each new process node requires new tool purchases, generating recurring upgrade cycles tied to Moore's Law progression.
semi-equip.whyFail: Export controls can strand revenue from key markets. Customers may extend tool lifetimes or reduce utilization if chip demand softens. A process node transition delay compresses equipment upgrade cycles. Geopolitical pressure could accelerate indigenous tool development in restricted markets.
semi-equip.bottleneck: Extreme ultraviolet lithography supply chain depth and the availability of specialized optical and laser components are the binding technical constraints. A handful of critical sub-suppliers create single points of failure across the industry.
semi-equip.metrics:
Wafer fabrication equipment spending (quarterly, by segment)
Tool lead times and backlog-to-revenue ratios
Utilization rates at leading-edge fabs
Export license approval rates and denied-order disclosures
semi-equip.redFlags:
Broad expansion of export control entity lists covering key customers
Fab customers publicly extending tool depreciation lives
Emerging indigenous tool vendors qualifying at leading-edge nodes
Sharp inventory corrections at major chipmakers reducing near-term orders
Concentration of revenue in one geography exceeding historical share

ai-data.name: AI data / labeling / synthetic data
ai-data.what: Training-data sourcing, labeling and synthetic data — fuel for the models.
ai-data.whyMoney: Model quality depends on data volume, diversity, and labeling accuracy. Providers who aggregate licensed content, operate scalable labeling pipelines, or generate validated synthetic data capture recurring fees as model developers continuously retrain and fine-tune. Proprietary datasets create switching costs.
ai-data.whyFail: Synthetic data generation is increasingly automated, compressing labeling margins. Legal uncertainty around training data licensing could invalidate existing contracts or require costly re-sourcing. Open datasets and self-supervised learning reduce dependence on labeled data over time.
ai-data.bottleneck: Legal clarity on copyright and data licensing is the binding adoption constraint. Without settled law or enforceable licensing frameworks, enterprise buyers face liability risk that slows procurement of third-party training data.
ai-data.metrics:
Volume of licensed training data under active contracts (tokens or records)

Race-to-the-bottom pricing in commodity labeling markets
Customer concentration in a small number of large model developers

observability.name: Observability / security / AI ops
observability.what: Monitoring, security and AI-ops — recurring software riding workload growth.
observability.whyMoney: As AI workloads grow in complexity and regulatory scrutiny, operators must monitor performance, detect anomalies, and secure inference pipelines. Vendors capture value through per-seat or consumption-based SaaS contracts that expand automatically with workload growth, creating net revenue retention above 100%.
observability.whyFail: Cloud hyperscalers bundle native observability and security tools, undercutting standalone vendors on price and integration. Open-source alternatives reduce willingness to pay. AI-specific monitoring is nascent; if model behavior becomes more predictable, perceived need may shrink.
observability.bottleneck: Integration complexity across heterogeneous AI stacks is the binding adoption constraint. Customers delay deployment when instrumentation requires significant engineering effort across multiple frameworks, clouds, and hardware types.
observability.metrics:
Net revenue retention rate
AI-specific workload monitoring seats or endpoints under contract
Mean time to detect and resolve AI inference anomalies
Security incident rates in monitored vs. unmonitored AI deployments
observability.redFlags:
Hyperscaler native tools gaining dominant share in enterprise surveys
Rapid commoditization of core metrics collection via open-source projects
Customer churn accelerating as AI stacks consolidate onto fewer platforms
Regulatory frameworks not materializing, reducing compliance-driven demand
Vendor inability to support new model architectures within a reasonable release cycle

databases.name: Databases / data platforms
databases.what: Data platforms and analytics where AI workloads actually live and query.
databases.whyMoney: AI applications require low-latency retrieval, vector search, and scalable analytics tightly coupled to model inference. Database vendors capture value through consumption pricing that scales with query volume and data size, embedding themselves in production AI pipelines where switching costs are high.
databases.whyFail: Hyperscalers offer integrated data and AI platforms that reduce the need for independent database vendors. Open-source engines with cloud wrappers compress margins. If AI workloads consolidate onto a small number of dominant platforms, niche database vendors lose addressable market.
databases.bottleneck: Vector search and real-time retrieval at scale remain engineering challenges; performance at billion-scale embedding indexes without cost explosion is the binding technical constraint limiting enterprise adoption of retrieval-augmented generation architectures.
databases.metrics:
Query volume and data under management growth rates
Net revenue retention and expansion revenue from existing customers
Vector search benchmark performance at scale (latency, recall, cost)
Share of AI production workloads using retrieval-augmented generation
databases.redFlags:
Hyperscalers releasing competitive vector and analytics features at no incremental cost
Open-source projects matching commercial performance benchmarks
Customer consolidation onto single-vendor AI platforms that exclude third-party databases
Pricing pressure driving gross margin compression below sustainable levels
Slow enterprise adoption of retrieval-augmented generation reducing vector database demand

edge.name: Edge AI / devices
edge.what: On-device and edge inference silicon — AI beyond the data center.
edge.whyMoney: Latency, privacy, and bandwidth constraints create demand for inference at the device or network edge. Silicon vendors and platform providers capture value through chip sales, per-device licensing, and software stacks that lock in OEM design wins across automotive, industrial, and consumer device cycles.
edge.whyFail: Edge AI silicon is fragmented across many use cases with different power, cost, and performance requirements. Cloud inference costs may fall fast enough to eliminate the economic case for on-device processing. Long OEM design cycles mean revenue lags investment by years.
edge.bottleneck: Power envelope and memory bandwidth at the device level are the binding physical constraints. Delivering sufficient model capability within milliwatt budgets for battery-powered devices requires architectural innovation that is not guaranteed on any fixed timeline.
edge.metrics:
Edge AI chip unit shipments by end market (automotive, industrial, consumer)
On-device inference performance per milliwatt (benchmark scores)
OEM design win announcements and time-to-revenue estimates
Share of AI inference workloads running at edge vs. cloud
edge.redFlags:
Cloud inference pricing declining faster than edge silicon cost curves
OEM customers delaying or canceling AI feature integration in product roadmaps
A dominant incumbent locking up key OEM design wins across multiple verticals
Regulatory restrictions on on-device data processing in key markets
Model size growth outpacing edge memory and compute improvements

robotics.name: Robotics / autonomy
robotics.what: Physical AI — autonomy, surgical and industrial robotics; long-dated moonshots.
robotics.whyMoney: Autonomy converts scarce skilled labor into scalable machine capacity. Operators who deploy reliable physical AI can expand output without proportional headcount growth, creating durable unit-economics advantages. Vendors capture value through hardware margins, recurring software licenses, and data-network effects that widen as fleet size grows.
robotics.whyFail: Structural failure modes include: liability regimes that stall commercial deployment; sensor or actuator reliability falling short of safety thresholds; integration complexity that raises total cost of ownership above human alternatives; and winner-take-all platform dynamics that commoditize hardware vendors while concentrating value in software layers.
robotics.bottleneck: The binding constraint is real-world data scarcity for edge-case training combined with actuator reliability at production scale. Simulation-to-reality transfer gaps mean robots trained in software often fail in unstructured environments, and high-precision mechanical components face supply and quality-control limits that slow fleet deployment.
robotics.metrics:
Fleet uptime rate (target threshold varies by application)
Mean time between failures per unit
Software attach rate and recurring revenue as % of total revenue
Customer payback period vs. human-labor alternative
Regulatory approval milestones by jurisdiction
robotics.redFlags:
Gross margins declining as hardware competition intensifies
High customer churn or pilot-to-production conversion below expectations
Regulatory moratoria or liability rulings in key markets
Over-reliance on a single end-market or anchor customer
Capex intensity rising faster than revenue growth

financing.name: Financing / private infrastructure capital
financing.what: Private capital and infra funds underwriting the capex — fee-rich but exposed if the cycle rolls over.
financing.whyMoney: Private infrastructure funds earn management fees on committed capital and carried interest on realized returns. AI infrastructure assets—data centers, power, fiber—offer long-duration contracted cash flows that match institutional liability profiles. Fee streams are relatively stable across the cycle; carry is the cyclical variable that amplifies upside when asset values rise.
financing.whyFail: Structural failure modes include: rising interest rates compressing asset valuations and making refinancing costly; hyperscaler demand softening faster than long-term leases can be renegotiated; power and land constraints preventing deployment of committed capital; and vintage concentration risk if multiple funds underwrite similar assets at peak valuations simultaneously.
financing.bottleneck: The binding constraint is the availability of permitted, powered sites. Grid interconnection queues, zoning approvals, and water rights for cooling create multi-year lead times that can strand committed capital or force deployment into inferior locations, pressuring projected returns before a single server is racked.
financing.metrics:
Debt-service coverage ratio on underlying assets
Weighted average lease term remaining across portfolio
Loan-to-value ratios at origination vs. current appraisal
Capital deployment pace vs. fund commitment schedule
Power capacity secured as % of total planned capacity
financing.redFlags:
Refinancing walls clustering in a narrow time window
Tenant concentration above acceptable thresholds in a single hyperscaler
Grid interconnection approvals delayed beyond underwritten timelines
Fund leverage ratios rising without corresponding revenue lock-in
Secondary-market discounts widening on fund interests

AIP.businessDesc: Arteris licenses network-on-chip (NoC) interconnect IP and SoC integration software. Its fabric is the on-chip road system that moves data between CPU, GPU/NPU, memory and I/O blocks inside a complex chip.
AIP.moat: Sticky design-time IP: once a NoC is architected into a chip it stays for the life of that program and its derivatives. Per-chip royalties stack on top of license ACV; deep integration and a hard-to-replicate IP library raise switching costs.
AIP.revGrowth: Annual contract value (ACV) growing double digits. Royalty revenue lags design wins by two to three years and is set to inflect as won designs reach volume production.
AIP.margins: IP-licensing model with very high gross margin. Opex-heavy on R&D and sales, so operating leverage arrives as ACV scales.
AIP.fcfPath: Approaching FCF breakeven. The royalty ramp is the path to durable free cash flow as cumulative design wins ship.
AIP.custQuality: Broad customer base across AI, data-center, automotive and chiplet designers, with a rising royalty footprint as designs reach production.
AIP.aiExposure: AI and chiplet complexity explode the number of on-chip connections. More accelerators, more HBM and more chiplets means more NoC content per design; UCIe and die-to-die interconnect are direct beneficiaries.
AIP.valRisk: Small-cap valued on forward ACV and royalty growth. Sensitive to design-win cadence and market risk-appetite; the multiple is volatile.
AIP.bull: Royalty inflection plus chiplet and NoC content growth turns a sticky IP base into compounding, capital-light licensing revenue that survives an overbuild.
AIP.bear: Design-win timing slips, royalties under-deliver, or a larger IP vendor (or in-house NoC) compresses pricing. Small-cap liquidity and dilution add risk.
AIP.prove: Accelerating ACV, royalty revenue inflecting upward, marquee AI and data-center design wins reaching production, and a clean march to positive FCF.
AIP.breakThesis: Stalling ACV, repeated royalty disappointments, key customers moving in-house or to a rival NoC, or persistent cash burn forcing dilution.

CBRS.bull: Wafer-scale engine architecture targets inference workloads where memory bandwidth and latency matter; if the design proves superior for specific AI tasks, it earns a durable niche against GPU incumbents.
CBRS.bear: Concentration in a narrow customer set and unproven free cash flow generation mean any design-win loss or hyperscaler preference shift could rapidly erode the revenue base before the company reaches self-funding scale.
CBRS.prove: Evidence to seek: expanding customer diversity beyond current base, gross margin expansion toward software-like levels, and positive free cash flow inflection signaling the cost structure is maturing.
CBRS.breakThesis: Thesis weakens if hyperscalers or sovereign AI customers publicly shift inference workloads back to GPU incumbents, or if gross margins compress materially, suggesting pricing power is absent.

BAM.fcfPath: TTM free cash flow ≈ $2.9B (Yahoo Finance, retrieved 2026-06-30)
BAM.aiExposure: Exposure comes through financing / private infrastructure capital: Private capital and infra funds underwriting the capex — fee-rich but exposed if the cycle rolls over.
BAM.bull: BAM earns recurring fee-related earnings on long-duration infrastructure, renewable power, and real estate AUM, with strong revenue growth suggesting successful capital formation across institutional and retail channels.
BAM.bear: As a subsidiary of Brookfield Corporation, BAM's fundraising and deal flow depend heavily on parent relationships; any parent-level stress or governance conflict could impair independent capital-raising credibility.
BAM.prove: Evidence to seek: continued double-digit fee-bearing capital growth, new flagship fund closes above prior vintages, and expanding distribution partnerships broadening the retail investor base.
BAM.breakThesis: Thesis weakens if fee-bearing AUM growth decelerates sharply, parent Brookfield Corporation faces balance-sheet strain that diverts institutional attention, or gross margins compress indicating rising cost of distribution.

KKR.businessDesc: KKR & Co. Inc. is a private equity and real estate investment firm specializing in direct and fund of fund investments.
KKR.aiExposure: Exposure comes through financing / private infrastructure capital: Private capital and infra funds underwriting the capex — fee-rich but exposed if the cycle rolls over.
KKR.bull: KKR's integrated model spanning private equity, infrastructure, real estate, and credit creates cross-platform capital deployment advantages, with insurance balance sheet assets providing a permanent capital base for fee generation.
KKR.bear: Recent revenue contraction signals that realized carry and transaction fees are cyclically sensitive; a prolonged exit market closure would suppress performance income and slow the deployment of dry powder.
KKR.prove: Evidence to seek: recovery in buyout exit activity, growth in insurance-sourced investable assets, and new infrastructure fund closes demonstrating LP confidence after the revenue decline.
KKR.breakThesis: Thesis weakens if the insurance integration strategy faces regulatory capital constraints, gross margins continue to compress, or fundraising for new flagship vehicles falls materially short of prior vintages.

APO.businessDesc: Apollo Global Management, Inc. is a private equity firm specializing in investments in credit, private equity, infrastructure, secondaries and real estate markets. The firm prefers to invest in private and public markets.
APO.aiExposure: Exposure comes through financing / private infrastructure capital: Private capital and infra funds underwriting the capex — fee-rich but exposed if the cycle rolls over.
APO.bull: Apollo's differentiated credit-first model, anchored by Athene's insurance liabilities, provides a large permanent capital base that funds yield-oriented strategies largely independent of traditional fundraising cycles.
APO.bear: Revenue contraction and thin gross margins suggest earnings are sensitive to credit spread movements and realized gains; a credit cycle downturn could impair Athene's portfolio and constrain Apollo's deployment capacity.
APO.prove: Evidence to seek: stabilization and recovery in fee-related earnings, growth in origination volumes across direct lending and structured credit, and Athene liability growth indicating continued insurance channel strength.
APO.breakThesis: Thesis weakens if credit losses in Athene's portfolio rise materially, regulatory scrutiny of insurance-linked alternative asset models intensifies, or gross margins fail to recover toward peer levels over multiple periods.

ARES.businessDesc: Ares Management Corporation operates as an alternative asset manager. Its Direct Lending Group segment provides financing solutions to small-to-medium sized companies. The company's Private Equity Group segment specializes in early venture, turnaround, mid venture, late venture, recapitalization, growth capital, middle market, mezzanine, distressed and growth buyouts.
ARES.fcfPath: TTM free cash flow ≈ $1.8B (Yahoo Finance, retrieved 2026-06-30)
ARES.aiExposure: Exposure comes through financing / private infrastructure capital: Private capital and infra funds underwriting the capex — fee-rich but exposed if the cycle rolls over.
ARES.bull: Ares' direct lending focus on middle-market companies generates predictable fee and interest income with strong revenue growth, as banks' retreat from leveraged lending structurally expands the addressable private credit market.
ARES.bear: Concentration in middle-market direct lending exposes Ares to elevated default risk in an economic downturn, where smaller borrowers have less financial flexibility than large-cap peers, potentially impairing credit performance.
ARES.prove: Evidence to seek: continued strong fee-bearing AUM growth, stable or improving credit quality metrics across the direct lending portfolio, and new fund closes demonstrating institutional demand for private credit strategies.
ARES.breakThesis: Thesis weakens if middle-market default rates rise meaningfully, gross margins compress as competition intensifies in direct lending, or free cash flow generation deteriorates despite strong headline revenue growth.

NVDA.businessDesc: Designs the GPUs, networking (NVLink/InfiniBand/Spectrum-X) and CUDA software stack that virtually all frontier AI training and most inference runs on. Sells full systems (racks, not chips) to hyperscalers, neoclouds, enterprises and sovereigns.
NVDA.moat: CUDA's 15-year software ecosystem plus co-designed networking makes the platform, not the chip, the product. Annual architecture cadence keeps rivals aiming at last year's target; supply relationships (TSMC, HBM, CoWoS) lock scarce inputs.
NVDA.revGrowth: Data-center revenue still growing strongly off an enormous base, driven by each architecture cycle and inference demand scaling with model deployment.
NVDA.margins: Gross margins in the 70s — extraordinary for hardware and the single biggest bear target. Software/networking attach defends them.
NVDA.fcfPath: Tens of billions of FCF per quarter; buybacks plus strategic investments (neoclouds, ecosystem) recycle it into demand for its own chips.
NVDA.custQuality: Concentrated: a handful of hyperscalers plus OpenAI/Meta drive most revenue — top-tier credit but real order-timing risk. Sovereign and enterprise demand slowly diversifies.
NVDA.aiExposure: It IS the buildout — every layer below exists to feed it and every layer above rents its output. Purest possible exposure, both directions.
NVDA.valRisk: Multiple is reasonable on forward earnings only if margins and growth hold; any capex digestion quarter re-rates it violently.
NVDA.bull: Inference demand compounds beyond training; networking + software become the margin story; the annual cadence keeps ASPs rising through the decade.
NVDA.bear: Hyperscaler ASICs take meaningful share, margins mean-revert toward hardware norms, and one capex air pocket reveals cyclicality the multiple never priced.
NVDA.prove: Sustained data-center growth with GM holding >70% while ASIC share stays contained; inference revenue visibly offsetting any training slowdown.
NVDA.breakThesis: Gross margin trending below 65%, a top customer materially shifting to in-house silicon, or purchase-commitment write-downs signaling overbuild.

CEG.businessDesc: Largest US nuclear fleet — clean, firm, 24/7 baseload power. Signs long-dated premium PPAs with hyperscalers (Microsoft/Crane restart) and sells into tightening grids.
CEG.moat: Existing nuclear capacity is irreplaceable on any relevant timeline: no one can build competing 24/7 carbon-free supply this decade. Relicensed, uprated, and sited near load.
CEG.revGrowth: Contracted step-ups as PPAs reprice legacy merchant output; data-center deals add premium tenor.
CEG.margins: Not a GM story — spread between fleet cost and realized power price, increasingly locked by contracts.
CEG.fcfPath: Strong and increasingly visible as contracts replace merchant exposure; nuclear PTC floors the downside.
CEG.custQuality: Hyperscaler counterparties on decade-plus PPAs — the best credit in the power world.
CEG.aiExposure: The purest scarcity play in the stack: AI load growth versus a fixed supply of firm clean power. Every datacenter announcement tightens its market.
CEG.valRisk: Re-rated from utility to growth multiple; priced for continued premium PPA flow and favorable co-location rules.
CEG.bull: Each new PPA re-marks the whole fleet's value; uprates and restarts add megawatts at incumbent economics; PTC floor limits downside.
CEG.bear: FERC/state rulings restrict behind-the-meter deals, AI load growth disappoints, or power prices mean-revert taking merchant upside with them.
CEG.prove: More hyperscaler PPAs at premium prices, co-location precedents clearing, realized prices climbing on repricing.
CEG.breakThesis: Adverse regulatory precedent on co-location, a demand air pocket softening power markets, or PPA flow stopping.

ANET.businessDesc: Data-center Ethernet switching leader: EOS (single binary OS) plus merchant-silicon switches run the front-end and increasingly the AI back-end networks of hyperscalers.
ANET.moat: EOS software quality and operational tooling — network engineers standardize on it and don't leave; deep co-design with Microsoft/Meta; open-Ethernet standard-bearer as AI fabrics move off InfiniBand.
ANET.revGrowth: AI back-end wins layering on top of steady cloud/enterprise growth; guidance keeps proving conservative.
ANET.margins: GM low-to-mid 60s, industry-best operating margins; software economics on hardware revenue.
ANET.fcfPath: Consistently strong, huge net cash, buybacks; a compounding machine financially.
ANET.custQuality: Microsoft and Meta are a huge revenue share — hyperscaler concentration is the permanent asterisk.
ANET.aiExposure: Direct: every GPU cluster needs a back-end fabric, Ethernet is winning the standard war, and content per GPU rises with cluster scale.
ANET.valRisk: Premium multiple that assumes both AI back-end share gains and no in-sourcing event.
ANET.bull: Ethernet displaces InfiniBand across AI fabrics, new AI titles (Oracle, neoclouds, sovereigns) diversify concentration, 800G→1.6T cycles lift ASPs.
ANET.bear: A top-two customer in-sources switching (white-box + SONiC) or shifts share to NVIDIA's Spectrum-X bundle; growth resets hard.
ANET.prove: Named new AI customers, back-end share gains at 800G/1.6T, and revenue beats sustained without customer-mix deterioration.
ANET.breakThesis: Microsoft or Meta visibly moving switching in-house, or NVDA bundling networking with GPUs squeezing merchant Ethernet out of AI deals.

CRDO.businessDesc: Connectivity silicon for AI clusters: Active Electrical Cables (AEC), SerDes retimers and optical DSPs that keep signals alive at 112G/224G as copper hits physical limits.
CRDO.moat: SerDes engineering at the bleeding edge with lower power than rivals — AECs became the default rack-scale interconnect and Credo owns the category it created.
CRDO.revGrowth: Hypergrowth: AEC adoption spreading across hyperscalers, with 1.6T generation and PCIe retimers extending the runway.
CRDO.margins: Gross margin mid-60s and rising with scale — genuinely software-like economics for a chip company.
CRDO.fcfPath: Recently inflected positive; small absolute numbers but the operating leverage is visible each quarter.
CRDO.custQuality: Extremely concentrated — a few hyperscalers dominate revenue and order timing; each new named customer materially de-risks the story.
CRDO.aiExposure: Content scales with cluster size and speed transitions: every GPU generation needs more, faster, lower-power interconnect. Pure per-GPU content growth story.
CRDO.valRisk: Priced as a hypergrowth small/mid cap — extreme multiple compression risk on any order pause, real upside torque while the ramp holds.
CRDO.bull: AECs become standard across all hyperscalers, 1.6T transition doubles content, customer base broadens from three to six-plus.
CRDO.bear: An anchor customer redesigns around them or dual-sources; one pushed-out quarter cracks the multiple in half.
CRDO.prove: Sequential growth with customer diversification disclosed; 1.6T design wins converting; margins holding through the ramp.
CRDO.breakThesis: Anchor-customer order pause, a credible AEC second source taking share, or the optical transition leapfrogging copper faster than expected.

AMD.businessDesc: The credible second source in AI compute: MI-series accelerators plus EPYC server CPUs (share-gaining) and embedded/client franchises. ROCm is the CUDA alternative hyperscalers actively fund.
AMD.moat: Chiplet design leadership and x86 server incumbency; the moat in AI is really the customer's desire for a second source — a strategic moat someone else maintains.
AMD.revGrowth: Data-center compounding on EPYC share and MI ramps; MI revenue growing but still a fraction of NVDA's.
AMD.margins: GM ~50%, diluted by GPU mix — the bear's favorite line item; improves if MI pricing and software mature.
AMD.fcfPath: Positive and improving; spends heavily on the software gap (acquisitions, ROCm engineering).
AMD.custQuality: Hyperscalers seeding MI deployments as negotiating leverage against NVDA — real revenue, but strategically motivated demand.
AMD.aiExposure: High but second-derivative: wins share only where customers force diversification; owns the 'NVDA at half price' slot in every RFP.
AMD.valRisk: Cheaper than NVDA on every metric for a reason; re-rates on MI credibility, de-rates on roadmap slips.
AMD.bull: MI roadmap executes annually, ROCm reaches good-enough for inference at scale, and even 15% accelerator share is transformative to earnings.
AMD.bear: The software gap never closes, MI stays a bargaining chip, and gross margin dilutes while R&D chases a moving target.
AMD.prove: Named MI deployments expanding generation-over-generation with GM stable; inference share data showing real traction.
AMD.breakThesis: A skipped or slipped MI generation, hyperscalers going ASIC-plus-NVDA-only, or GM eroding below the high-40s.

MRVL.businessDesc: Custom ASIC design partner (the other arms dealer besides Broadcom) plus electro-optics (PAM4 DSPs), switching and storage silicon — connectivity and custom compute for hyperscalers.
MRVL.moat: One of two companies with the SerDes/packaging IP and design muscle to deliver hyperscaler ASICs; optics DSP franchise rides every optical transition.
MRVL.revGrowth: AI revenue (custom + optics) growing fast; custom programs ramp in steps as each generation reaches production.
MRVL.margins: GM ~60% with custom silicon slightly dilutive; operating leverage as AI mix rises.
MRVL.fcfPath: Solid and improving with data-center mix; R&D intensity stays high by necessity.
MRVL.custQuality: A few hyperscalers dominate — program wins and losses move the stock violently in both directions.
MRVL.aiExposure: Custom silicon plus optical interconnect are both pure AI-buildout categories; content grows with cluster scale and the ASIC diversification trend.
MRVL.valRisk: Priced on AI custom-silicon expectations; program-timing disappointments have repeatedly gapped the stock.
MRVL.bull: Custom programs multiply as every hyperscaler wants its own silicon, optics content compounds with 1.6T, and AI becomes most of revenue.
MRVL.bear: Broadcom takes the marquee programs, a key customer in-sources or cancels, and legacy segments keep dragging.
MRVL.prove: New custom program disclosures with production ramps on schedule; optics share holding through the 1.6T transition.
MRVL.breakThesis: A flagship custom program lost to Broadcom or in-house teams; optics share erosion to competitors.

checklistTemplate.text: Is the original thesis still intact, or did the story actually change?
Has the underlying bottleneck loosened (supply caught up, scarcity gone)?
Is the decline driven by dilution or debt — not just sentiment?
Did a key customer or design win leave?
Is the monetization tag still valid (scarcity / licensing vs capex-financed)?
Am I adding because of analysis — or because it is red?
Would I buy this today at this price if I held none?
Is position sizing still within my risk limit after averaging down?
